fact_en: Biodegradable waste like fruit peels and leaves can be made into compost — a natural fertilizer that helps plants grow big and strong!
fact_bis: Ang madunot nga basura sama sa panit sa prutas ug dahon mahimong himoon nga compost — usa ka natural nga abono nga makatabang sa pagtubo nga maayo sa mga tanom!

findings.note: title_bis "Compost Balat Dahon Pataba" — in Cebuano balat = SEA CUCUMBER (trepang); fruit peel is panit, which the body uses correctly ("panit sa prutas"). Tagalog false friend in the headline, so the compost card is headlined with a sea animal. Same title also uses Tagalog pataba for fertilizer where the body says abono; terms list is the Tagalog one ("balat ng prutas", "pataba"), which is how the title drifted.

fact_en: Paper loves to soak up water! But when it gets wet, it becomes very weak and tears easily.
fact_bis: Ganahan mosuyop og tubig ang papel! Pero kung mabasa kini, mahumok ug sayon mapunit.

findings.note: Tagalog false friend: EN "when it gets wet, it becomes very weak and tears easily" -> BIS "mahumok ug sayon mapunit". In Cebuano punit = to PICK UP with the fingers (tear is gisi/magisi); punit only means tear in Tagalog. The Cebuano reads 'wet paper becomes soft and is easy to pick up' - the opposite implication for fragility - and nothing else in the card restores the tearing fact.

title_bis: Mineral gikan sa Bato sa Apog
fact_en:
How does water become hard?

It happens when water flows through limestone rocks, dissolving calcium and magnesium from them!
fact_bis:
Giunsa pagkahigot ang tubig?

Mahitabo kini kung moagi ang tubig sa mga batong-apog, matunaw niini ang calcium ug magnesium!

findings.note: Q: EN "How does water become hard?" -> BIS "Giunsa pagkahigot ang tubig?". Cebuano higot = to TIE/bind; hard is gahi/tig-a (used correctly in every neighbouring hard-water card). Nothing in this card names hardness at all: title_bis is "Mineral gikan sa Bato sa Apog" and the answer only says calcium and magnesium dissolve from limestone. A child is left with an unanswerable question ('how does water get tied?') and never learns this is how water becomes hard water.

fact_en:
Does a burning candle really lose mass?

Nope! The burning wax just turns into gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor that escape into the air.
fact_bis:
Mawala ba gyud ang masa sa nasunog nga kandila?

Dili! Ang nasunog nga talo nahimong gas sama sa carbon dioxide ug water vapor nga miikyas sa hangin.

findings.note: title_bis "Kandila Gas nga Mobalik" for "Candle Gas Escapes" — mobalik = comes BACK, the opposite of the card's point that the burnt wax leaves as gas (body: "miikyas sa hangin"). The headline reverses the direction of the fact the card teaches.

fact_en:
Do same-sized objects always have the same mass?

Nope! Two things of the same size can have different masses, like a steel ball and a cotton ball.
fact_bis:
Kanunay ba nga parehas ang masa sa duha ka butang nga parehas og gidak-on?

Dili! Duha ka butang nga parehas og gidak-on mahimong managlahi og masa, sama sa bola nga puthaw ug bola nga bulak.

findings.note: EN example is "a steel ball and a cotton ball"; bis says "bola nga puthaw ug bola nga bulak". In Cebuano bulak = FLOWER (cotton = gapas; Tagalog false friend, and this same batch correctly uses gapas in ffct-16597/16598/16613). Nothing else in the card restores cotton, so the child gets a "flower ball" as the light same-size object.

fact_en: Some fabrics are natural like cotton, while others are synthetic like nylon and polyester. Synthetic fabric dries faster but can feel hotter to wear!
fact_bis: Ang ubang panapton natural sama sa gapas, ug ang uban synthetic sama sa nylon ug polyester. Mas paspas mamala ang synthetic apan mas init isul-ob!

findings.note: title_bis "Bulak ug Nylon Tela" for "Natural vs Synthetic Fabric" — headline reads "Flower and Nylon Fabric"; bulak = flower in Cebuano, cotton = gapas (the body itself uses gapas, so the title contradicts its own card).

fact_en: Many foods like bread and meat turn brown and smell much richer when they are heated strongly!
fact_bis: Daghang pagkaon sama sa pan ug karne mahimong brown ug mas humot kon initon pag-ayo!

findings.note: title_bis "Kayumanggi ug Baho nga Pagkaon" for "Food Browns Heated" (EN: heated food "smells much richer"). Baho in Cebuano is a FOUL smell, so the headline asserts heated food stinks - the opposite of the card's point; the body has it right with "mas humot". (Kayumanggi is also Tagalog for brown, secondary.)

fact_en:
When does an object sink in water?

An object sinks when it is denser than the same amount of water!
fact_bis:
Kanus-a molunod ang usa ka butang sa tubig?

Molunod ang usa ka butang kon kini mas dasok o mas bug-at kay sa samang gidak-on sa tubig!

findings.note: title_bis "Labaw Siksik Lubog" for "Denser Objects Sink". Tagalog false friend: lubog = to sink in Tagalog, but in Cebuano lubog = murky/turbid (lapok nga tubig). The headline reads "denser = murky", naming a different property than sinking. Cebuano for sink is lunod/unlod, which the body uses correctly ("Molunod ang usa ka butang...").

fact_en:
Why do we stir water when mixing dye?

Diffusion alone is slow, so stirring the water mixes the dye much faster than diffusion by itself!
fact_bis:
Nganong nato kutawon ang tubig kon magbutang og tina?

Ang diffusion lang hinay, mao nga kon kutawon nato ang tubig, mas paspas mosagol ang tina kaysa diffusion lamang!

findings.note: title_bis "Diffusion Halok" for "Diffusion vs Stirring". Halok means KISS in Cebuano; the card is about stirring (kutaw), which the body uses correctly. The headline names a completely different thing and gives a child no handle on the stirring-vs-diffusion contrast the card teaches.

fact_en: Hot smoke always rises up! When escaping a fire, crawl low to the ground where the air is cleaner.
fact_bis: Kanunay mosaka ang init nga aso! Kung mokagiw sa sunog, kamang ka ubos diin mas limpyo ang hangin.

findings.note: title_bis "Kawat Ubos Usok Hangin" (en "Crawl Low Under Smoke"). In Cebuano kawat = to STEAL (or wire); crawl = kamang, which the body uses correctly ("kamang ka ubos"). The headline of a fire-escape safety card therefore reads "Steal Low ..." and gives no usable instruction. Same title also uses Tagalog usok for smoke where Cebuano is aso (body has aso) - secondary, not flagged separately.

title_bis: Pores Dakop sa Gadak-on sa Baho
fact_en: A water filter has tiny holes called pores. Water slips through, but dirt that's too big gets left behind—just like a strainer! The smaller the holes, the more dirt it catches.
fact_bis: Ang water filter adunay gagmay nga mga lungag nga gitawag og pores. Moagi ang tubig, pero mabilin ang hugaw nga sobrang dako—sama sa salaan! Kung mas gamay ang lungag, mas daghan ang masala nga hugaw.

findings.note: Title names a different thing: title_en "Pores Trap by Size" -> "Pores Dakop sa Gadak-on sa Baho" = "pores catch by the size of the SMELL". Baho is odour, not dirt (hugaw); same wrong-word swap as ffct-17115, in the headline a child sees.

title_bis: Balas Dakop sa Pino nga Baho
fact_en: The sand layer catches tiny dirt bits that slipped past bigger stones. Between sand grains are tiny gaps that trap fine dirt as water passes through!
fact_bis: Ang balas mosalo sa gagmay nga hugaw nga nakalusot sa dagkong bato. Tunga sa mga lugas sa balas naa gamay nga mga luna diin maipit ang pino nga hugaw samtang moagi ang tubig!

findings.note: Title names a different thing: title_en "Sand Catches Fine Dirt" -> "Balas Dakop sa Pino nga Baho". Baho = ODOUR/smell in Cebuano, not dirt (hugaw). The headline claims sand traps fine SMELLS — actively misleading next to the charcoal card in the same deck (ffct-17116), which is the one that removes smells.
